root_causes.description: The frontend container was forcibly stopped ('Killing: Stopping container frontend') and a replacement pod (frontend-76cbddfbcc-zm8l8) was scheduled, created and started within the incident window, indicating an abrupt frontend pod/container termination consistent with a pod crash. CPU, memory and error rate on frontend remained at baseline, ruling out resource-driven failure.

evidence.expected_baseline: no 'Killing/Stopping container' events for frontend under normal operation

evidence.observed_value: count=1 (new frontend pod created after termination)
evidence.expected_baseline: no new frontend pod creation events in steady state
no container start events in steady state

root_causes.description: A downstream dependency disruption cannot be fully excluded since frontend depends on checkout, recommendation, product-catalog, cart, shipping, currency and ad, but no error traces or error logs surfaced for frontend and error rates stayed at baseline, making this a weak secondary hypothesis.

evidence.expected_baseline: error traces expected if a dependency failure were propagating
error logs expected for dependency failures

root_causes.description: checkout is a downstream dependency of frontend and an initial error-rate sweep target; its error rate stayed at baseline, ruling it out as a propagating fault source.

remediation_steps: Inspect frontend pod logs and previous-container (--previous) logs for the terminated container 'frontend' to determine the exit code/reason for the kill.
Check frontend liveness/readiness probe configuration and restart policy; verify whether probes or an external eviction caused the container stop.
Confirm frontend replica count is >=2 so a single pod crash does not remove all serving capacity.
Review Kubernetes events and node conditions (kubectl describe pod frontend-76cbddfbcc-zm8l8) to rule out node pressure, OOMKill or eviction as the trigger.
Add alerting on kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total and 'Killing/Stopping container' events for frontend to catch future abrupt terminations.
